description: This History TV18 segment profiles Johny Hot Dog, a famous street-food outlet in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, India. The video opens by asking what today's most popular dish might be, then reveals it is not a multinational burger or pizza, but the Veg Hot Dog from this small shop. Founder Vijay Singh Rathore, age 60, explains he started selling the snack in 1978 after working in a tea shop, beginning with an investment of Rs. 500. The 'hot dog' contains no sausage; instead, it uses a soft bun filled with a fried potato (aloo tikki) patty, served with green chutney, red sauce, and onions. The video shows large-scale preparation — grating potatoes, mixing spices, forming and frying hundreds of patties daily on a giant griddle, and assembling them quickly for crowds. According to Uber Eats data from 2019, it was the most-ordered menu item in the APAC region, earning Rathore an award in Hong Kong. Customers, including locals who have eaten there since the 1980s and visitors from Mumbai, praise its taste and consistency. The shop serves over 3,000 per day, using around 200 kg of potatoes and 1,000 eggs daily. The piece highlights its enduring popularity across generations and its reputation as Indore's iconic vegetarian street food.

description:
This is a recipe reel by professional chef and food creator Nehal Karkera demonstrating how to make 'Dhuaan Dahi Mutton,' an Indian mutton curry. The video opens with raw mutton pieces labeled 'Mutton?' and then shows the finished dish titled on screen. The chef prepares a custom spice powder by dry-roasting coriander, black pepper, cumin, and other whole spices, then grinding them. He also preps sliced onions, green chilies, and a green paste of onion, garlic, and chili. Cooking starts with ghee in a pressure cooker, followed by whole spices, then the mutton which is 'bhunoed' (sautéed) repeatedly. The ground spice mix is added, then water, salt, and the cooker is sealed for 4-5 whistles. After cooking, whisked yogurt (dahi) and fresh mint are stirred in, the curry simmers to separate oil from gravy, and a traditional 'dhuaan' (smoke) tempering is done using hot coal and ghee covered for three minutes. The dish is finished with garam masala, chopped cilantro, ginger juliennes, and served in a bowl with roti. The chef eats it with his hands, pulls apart tender meat, and encourages viewers to tag others and repost. The tone is instructional, appetizing, and casual, emphasizing rich flavor and messy, hands-on eating.

description:
This is a Hindi-language cooking reel by food creator Kabita Singh (@kabitaskitchen) demonstrating how to make 'Palak Besan ki Sabzi,' presented as a tasty lunch or dinner option. The video opens with the finished dish—a thick orange-green spinach curry topped with butter—served on a steel thali with roti, pickle, and sliced onion, carrot, and beetroot. The recipe proceeds step-by-step: white sesame seeds (2 tbsp) and raw peanuts (1/2 cup) are dry-roasted for half a minute, then coarsely ground and set aside. In another pan, gram flour/besan (2 tbsp) is dry-roasted for one minute. For the curry, oil is heated, then hing (1/2 tsp), cumin seeds (1 tsp), chopped garlic, and green chilies are fried briefly, followed by 1/2 cup chopped onion cooked for 3 minutes. Chopped spinach (500 grams) and salt to taste are added and cooked for 2 minutes until wilted, then stirred for 4-5 minutes. Turmeric powder (1/2 tsp), red chili powder (1/2 tsp), and garam masala (1/2 tsp) are added and cooked for 30 seconds. The ground peanut-sesame powder and roasted besan are mixed in, then 1 cup water is added, mixed well, and simmered covered for 8-10 minutes. Finally, amchur powder (1/2 tsp) and 1 tsp butter are stirred in. The video ends with serving shots emphasizing the texture and presentation. The tone is instructional, warm, and appetizing, with no controversial or risky content.
